Mr. Chairman, checking back on the record of the discussion when this legislation first appeared before the house, I find that it is almost a year ago since we were having a similar debate. At that time many lengthy statements were made concerning it. From this side of the house the viewpoint was unanimous that this bill, called the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act, 1956, was not adequate to deal with the problem with which it professed to deal.
One of the main points I raised last year, I recall, was that the very wording of the bill, and of the resolution conveyed the wrong impression, in that it laid stress on the word "temporary". In the resolution we have before us again today there is a reference to this legislation as an interim financing act. In the events that have transpired during the past 12 months, when we have had some experience with the operation of the act, I find no reason at all to change the viewpoint I held last year. This viewpoint is not only determined by the recommendations we have received repeatedly from the farm organizations who are most intimately acquainted with the subject, but also from the individual farmers in my constituency.
The method the government has chosen to assist the farmer in the chronic cash shortage problem that has confronted him now for the past few years is totally inadequate to deal with the situation. I am afraid the government, in re-emphasizing the temporary nature of this type of assistance, is missing the point entirely. Just the other day we were dealing with another important piece of agricultural legislation, the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, and I was interested to note that this act was regarded as a temporary piece of legislation even though it has been on the statute books since 1939. Well, that is a rather long temporary period. I am afraid unless something is done in regard to the government's approach to the changed cash position of the farmer, if it continues to be regarded by the government as a temporary situation, we will find this piece of legislation still on the statute books 20 years hence as a temporary measure, much after the fashion of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
The arguments against this particular approach to the farmer's position have been recited repeatedly in this chamber. Most of the arguments have been placed on the record again by the speakers who have preceded me in this discussion today. But judging from the government's repeated attempts to solve the basic problem of agriculture by pro tern methods, it would appear that there is a need for something to be said again this afternoon concerning the basic problem of agriculture,

prairie agriculture in particular but also agriculture generally across the country. The information we have on this subject has been added to by the recent submission of the preliminary report of the Gordon commission.
The section of this report dealing with agriculture, the third chapter on page 25, begins by saying:
Great changes have taken place in Canadian agriculture since the end of the last war. Between 1946 and 1955 the physical volume of output per farm has increased by 30 per cent and gross physical output per man-hour by almost 75 per cent. This greater productivity has been made possible in part by favourable weather conditions in western Canada and, in part, by substantial increases in the use of power and equipment on farms.
That is as far as I intend to go in quoting from the Gordon commission report in this respect, but hon. members who have read the report in detail know that the general thesis that is put forward in that analysis is that the agricultural industry in Canada has passed through a basic change in the past two decades. Agriculture has moved from a subsistence economy and is now operating on a straight cash basis, as is the case with small businesses and other industrial activities in Canada.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the government fails to appreciate the fundamental change that has taken place in our economy. The farmer needs cash if he is going to carry on a successful and efficient farm operation today. The surplus situation we have had with us during the past few years, which has been partly created by unduly heavy yields, is also due to the changed methods of production, and in certain respects to a proportionate loss of the total world market for grain. It appears that this surplus situation is going to be with us for some considerable years. This is not necessarily a bad thing, as the hon. member for Battle River-Camrose has just suggested, but it does mean that the parliament of Canada must take some action to deal with the special problems created for our grain producers by this continuing condition.
The interim finance act as a method of getting cash into the hands of the hard-pressed farmer is merely one way of solving this problem. It is the over-all situation that will have to be met with over-all planning on the part of the government of Canada. This is merely one very small contribution to solving the total difficulty. The basic difficulty is the necessity of providing stability of income for the farmer as we have provided stability of income for other segments of the national economy by various devices, most of which have been devised on the national level of government.

Another aspect of the difficulty that has been pointed out from time to time in this house that suggests we are in the midst of a fundamental change is the continuing outcry for a more generous credit supply. We even have the farmers today suggesting that if they are to retain a supply of reliable labour for the farm a program similar to that of unemployment insurance for the industrial worker must be devised. Then again on this same point, emphasizing the fundamental need for a reliable source of income and a stable income if the farmer is to operate efficiently, there is the growing demand, particularly from our prairie farmers, for some kind of crop insurance which would help them meet the impact of the plagues and the pests to which the agricultural industry inevitably falls heir.
Then finally, Mr. Chairman, there is the continued demand for cash advances on farm-stored grain. I should point out that it comes not only from the farmers. In talking to the businessmen in the smaller communities of western Canada I find that they are feeling with equal force the lack of sufficient cash on the part of the farmers to meet current obligations. This whole problem has very broad sociological implications. We are faced with a situation of depopulation in the rural areas because of the expansion of our farms into increasingly larger units in order to meet the economic changes arising from the revolution taking place in agriculture. These changes in turn, of course, are leaving in their wake agricultural ghost communities all over the prairies as the farm population finds the pressure of rural-urban migration becoming increasingly intensified.
The principal objections to this one small contribution by the government to solving the farmer's problem have been laid down point by point here this afternoon. The very fact that in the minister's statement itself it has been said that limited use has been made of the legislation up to the present time suggests that it has not been received very cordially by the farmer. One objection last year toward cash advances was the point made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, that the wheat board officials were not interested in the cash advance solution to the farmer's problem of cash shortage.
I am glad to know that argument has not been used this year. In fact previous speakers in this debate, Mr. Chairman, have pointed out that actually the wheat board set-up, the very fact that we have the wheat board organization, makes it a fairly simple matter to have these cash advances made to our prairie farmers.
I have heard farmers use this argument repeatedly. His wheat is going to be marketed
Grain
eventually through the wheat board. He has no other recourse, as the situation exists, and he resents the necessity of having to go to the banks and meet his problem of cash shortage through the method provided by this legislation. He calls it a system under which he has to pay interest on his own wages. He is going to sell his grain eventually to the wheat board. The money is actually his. If the market were there, if the grain could be sold, the money would be as good as in his pocket, and he resents this rather complicated and awkward procedure. The farmer has always been reluctant to indulge in credit activities of this kind with the bank. Perhaps part of the difficulty is an educational one. He resents this complicated procedure to make it possible for him to have at least a minimum supply of cash to meet his current obligations.
The minister made the point that there had been some change in the attitude of the farmer toward the government's approach to this problem. I took the trouble to make some inquiries concerning the meeting which was held March 1 last in the city of Saskatoon. This meeting was called for the definite purpose of coming to some conclusions with regard to the legislation we now have before us. The legislation had been placed on the order paper, and the three federations in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the three unions, the three pools and representatives of the United Grain Growers came together at Saskatoon on March 1 to consider what attitude they might take in regard to this legislation. In conversations with some of the men who were at that gathering they very emphatically informed me that their position in regard to this legislation had not changed one iota. They still oppose it as a method of meeting the problem of cash shortage. They still insist that the cash advance formula would be a more effective and more efficient method of handling this situation.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort placed on record this afternoon the resolution that emerged from this particular meeting and it, without any equivocation at all, indicates that the farmer reluctantly consented to accept what the government was offering because at this late date there was no other alternative. The need is there, the basic problem is there, and it is better than nothing at all; but, as the preamble to the resolution says:
While we do not agree that the Prairie Grain Producers Interim Financing Act is the most satisfactory method for making money available on grain that cannot be delivered, however, in view of the late date in having a more satisfactory plan for cash advances adopted at this session of

Grain
parliament this committee recommends to the federal government the inclusion of the following amendments.
I wanted to place that on record because of the statement of the minister. There is no doubt about it, Mr. Chairman; the Canadian economy is booming. We have that drummed home in season and out of season by representatives of the government. It is rather tragic that in this booming economy a very important segment, if not the most important segment, our agricultural industry, finds itself in a state of considerable economic distress. There is no doubt, there is no uncertainty at all-and this has been underlined again by the Gordon commission-concerning the continuing development and increasing prosperity of our Canadian economy.
But I think the question does arise on the occasion of a discussion of this kind as to just what direction this boom is going to take. All hon. members of this committee should give serious consideration to moving in a more positive way to help the farmer.
The farmer is certainly doing everything within his means by way of recommendations, resolutions, briefs and pilgrimages to Ottawa to bring home to the government the economic situation of agriculture, and certainly we have heard enough speeches in this house which would tend to suggest that all is not well in our agricultural industry. If we are to continue to have a balanced, healthy economy, Mr. Chairman, I am quite convinced that something much more adequate than what we have before us must be devised to help the farmer to adjust to the economic situation in which he now finds himself.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the resolution before us in my opinion does nothing more than prolong an inadequate piece of legislation. The Minister of Trade and Commerce in opening his remarks today made a statement which at first I thought I had not heard well, because it was difficult to believe when he stated that this resolution together with the proposed amendments to the bill had met with the unanimous approval of the farm organizations.
I contend, sir, that the very opposite is the truth because, as the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris have already pointed out, as recently as March 1, 1957, the organizations representing grain producers in western Canada at a meeting in Saskatoon passed a resolution which very definitely stated the very opposite to what this committee was told this afternoon. The very first sentence of their resolution indicates their stand. It reads:
Resolved that while we do not agree that the Prairie Grain Producers' Interim Financing Act is

the most satisfactory method for making money available on grain that cannot be delivered-
Then it goes on to say that in view of the fact that they do not expect anything better at this time they propose certain amendments to the existing act.
While I am in thorough agreement with the first part of that resolution, in that I agree this is certainly not the best method, I am not quite so enthusiastic about the latter part of the resolution, which indicates that in view of the late date we cannot expect any action on cash advances. I do not think that is the case. I do not see any particular difficulty in the road of this parliament adopting a system of cash advances within the course of the next two or three days. In my opinion it would not take any longer for the minister to introduce legislation for the purpose of establishing a system of cash advances, as has been demanded by farm organizations for the past two or three years, than it will to pass this resolution which is like a French proverb which comes to mind; "the more it changes, the more it is the same". It does not do anything.
In order to establish more clearly what is the stand of the farm organizations I think I should put on record what their resolutions were as passed at their conventions and as outlined in their briefs presented to this government. I have in my hand the submissions made to the government on February 19, 1957, by the interprovincial farm union council. I propose to read their proposal which appears on page 8 of the submission under item No. 7, and I would like the committee to compare this with the statement made by the minister this afternoon that what he is proposing in this resolution has met with the approval of the farm organizations. This is their proposal:
That a permanent system of cash advances be established on the basis recommended in previous submissions, in order that farmers will have the means to meet their annual obligations-
Then it goes on:
-also, that provision be made for accelerated depreciation on grain storage buildings built by farmers.
The first part of that proposal is perfectly clear. This was the submission of the interprovincial farm union council to this government as late as February 19, 1957. The interprovincial farm union council includes the farm unions of five provinces, the three prairie provinces and also Ontario and British Columbia. That body, which represents a very large proportion of the grain producers in Canada, stated in clear language to the

government that what they want is a permanent system of cash advances; yet the minister tells us today they have approved something different.
Let me turn now to the attitude of the wheat pools. The wheat pools do business with the grain producers in the three prairie provinces, and in that way they also represent a great majority of the grain producers. In their statement of policy of January 19, 1956, here is what the Saskatchewan wheat pool had to say:
The current problem of a shortage of farm cash was considered as soon as the annual meeting opened. The delegates went on record in favour of a system of cash advances against farm stored grain to be paid out by the Canadian wheat board through elevator companies with the federal government assuming the interest on the loans involved.
Certainly that is clear and unequivocal enough. The delegates assembled in the biggest wheat pool meeting in the world passed a resolution in plain language stating that they are in favour of a system of cash advances through the Canadian wheat board, using the elevator agents as the channel of distribution, and that the federal government should absorb the interest on the loan involved.
Here we have two farm bodies between them representing, I think we can safely say, at least 90 per cent of the farmers in the prairie provinces, both stating clearly and categorically that what they want is a system of cash advances with the interest absorbed by the federal government. Instead of that the minister places on the order paper a resolution which in effect only continues the inadequate bank loan system we have had since it came into effect last year.
I say there is time to do something different because after all, as the resolution itself points out, authority is being sought from this house to enable the governor in council to make certain arrangements in order that bank loans guaranteed by the treasury may be made from the period September 1, 1957, to June 1, 1958. In other words this legislation will have no effect whatever until September 1 of this year. We are now in the middle of March, and there is plenty of time between now and September 1 to do what the grain producers are recommending.
Therefore I see no particular reason why, unless the government and particularly those hon. members who support the government are prepared to disregard completely the recommendations of the farm organizations, action should not be taken to put into effect a system of cash advances as has been recommended. I think it is up to the hon. members who support the government to see that
Grain
this responsibility is met, particularly those who come from the rural parts of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba and who more directly represent the cause of the farmers here.
Even the extension of this act seems to indicate that the government continues to view this question as a purely temporary problem, though one can refer to almost any publication which has had anything to do with farm problems during the last three years, whether it is the Gordon report, or the report of any other commission, or the briefs of farm organizations, and confirm that the farmers no longer regard this question of our grain surplus as a temporary problem. Certainly all the indications are that it is going to be a long-term problem, for various reasons.
First, and perhaps most important, is the fact that there has been a tremendous change in methods of production. Under normal conditions, Mr. Chairman, we can now expect greater yields per acre on the prairies than in the past. New and improved methods of farming, improved farm implements which enable farmers to develop their land properly, put in the seed at due time and gather the harvest at the proper time, when weather conditions permit, combined with the improved know-how of the farmers, are going to improve the yield per acre very materially. That in itself is a very good thing, because this country has always prided itself on being able to put out more production per man than perhaps any other country in the world with the possible exception of our great neighbour to the south; and today possibly we are even ahead of her. We take pride in being a high production country, and that is something which could make Canada a very prosperous and happy nation.
But are we not discouraging this most desirable element in our economy by not making provision for putting the farmer on a cash basis, which is the only way in which he can operate efficiently? The government has used various arguments in the past for not agreeing with our proposal for cash advances, and I am not going to take up the time of the committee by answering all those arguments. Some of them have already been referred to by other hon. members. But I find it hard to believe that the government can adopt two different attitudes at one and the same time in such glaring fashion as it does.
Less than a year ago parliament was advised of a proposition by the government to provide a cash advance to one corporation to the tune of about $80 million. That was to one private corporation, namely the Trans-Canada Pipe Line Company. With such great

Grain
enthusiasm did the government propose this that they were prepared to move closure and do almost anything in order to steamroller that measure through the house, in spite of the strong and bitter opposition which it encountered not only in the House of Commons but in the country generally.
However, when we come to this question, as soon as we propose cash advances the government begin to present their other side; they haul out their tight money policy. If there is anything that indicates a tight money policy it is this present legislation, because not only does it put a farmer in the position of having to practically beg at the doorstep of the bank for a loan, but under the proposed resolution the interest rate itself is no longer fixed. The resolution provides that from here on the interest shall be at a rate not to exceed an amount that is to be fixed by order in council.
What does that mean? In his introductory remarks today the minister did not indicate what the rate of interest would be, or what the government has in mind as a fair rate of interest. This gives rise to great anxiety because the trend, in the last six or eight months particularly, in response to the government's tight money policy has been for interest rates to notch up all along the line. Is the government going to apply this tight money policy to this act also, and provide that interest rates should rise by one-half or one-quarter of one per cent every few months, with the result that a farmer will not know from day to day what it is going to cost him to get a loan under this legislation?
I think that in itself is enough to make farmers look at this act with a great deal of anxiety from now on. In any case, farmers will be at the mercy of an order in council which could raise the interest rates at any time without notice, and I think before we are through with this legislation the minister should give the committee some indication of what he has in mind as a maximum interest rate under this act.
It has been pointed out that this legislation and the demand for cash advances arose out of the situation in this country with regard to grain surpluses. I have stated that in my opinion this is not a temporary situation, but that it is going to be a continuing problem. And I think if the government is really serious about providing a long-term solution to this problem, some steps must be taken along the lines of either this type of legislation or of cash advances.
At any rate some attempt must be made to face this question, and I think it is time for the government to say they are prepared to look upon the production of grain in this
[Mr. Zaplitny.l
country as a national asset. But they don't. We have referred in this house and elsewhere to the grain situation on the prairies as "a grain problem" or "a surplus problem". We refer to it as a problem. But I think that is looking at it in the wrong way. Properly considered, it is one of the greatest national assets we have. If we treated it properly our grain surplus would not be a problem but an asset, and if the government were prepared to regard it as an asset and make provision for orderly marketing and storage of that grain without placing the burden of financing it on the shoulders of the farmers who have produced it, it would become an asset.
Steps should have been taken long ago- certainly they should be taken now-to provide greater storage facilities, to provide for greater movement of grain and to arrange for a larger supply of boxcars so that this idea of a quota, which every year is a recurring headache, will eventually be done away with. The farmer will then be in the position of knowing that if nature has been bountiful, and he has produced a good crop, he will be able to market that crop at least within a reasonable period of time, let us say six or eight months. As it is now he does not know whether it will take him 12, 24 or even 36 months to dispose of his crop.
Each year when a good crop is in the making it is a joy to the farmers, but this most natural joy in the world is dampened by fear and anxiety as to how it will affect the surplus position.
I think those are steps that have to be taken. The government has to take a whole new look at the grain business. A new philosophy has to be evolved. The government has to treat our grain as a national asset, and every surplus should be a matter of joy to the government, not something to be treated as a problem that has to be faced from year to year.
There is another reason why in my opinion the whole question of cash advances is very important to western farmers. Not long ago in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Moose Mountain, I believe, the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated that the Canadian farmer has been in competition with the United States treasury for quite some time now. The minister showed no particular surprise at that situation, as if it was to be expected. That may be the case. But if, as the minister admits, the Canadian farmer today is in competition in the disposal of his grain with the United States treasury, which is involved to a far greater extent in the disposal of grain than is the case in Canada, is that not all the more reason why the national treasury or the

government of Canada must move in on the side of the Canadian farmer if he is to have any chance whatever in the face of competition with the United States treasury, which the minister admits to be the case?
What form of competition is it? In the United States there is the Commodity Credit Corporation, which is financed by the national treasury and is authorized to take from the farmer on a cash basis all the grain he grows. They go to the farmer and pay him approximately $2.24 a bushel for his wheat. He can either deliver the grain to the Commodity Credit Corporation if the corporation has space in which to store it or, if it is more convenient, the farmer is permitted to build approved storage on his farm. He is then paid so much per bushel per month for the grain while it is in his own storage waiting to be delivered to the Commodity Credit Corporation.
In driving through the United States last summer I had the opportunity to stop and examine some of these farms where approved storage has been built, and I spoke with some of the farmers about it. I find that the farmer there approves strongly of the method, because it does two things at once. It provides him with a cash return immediately as soon as he produces his grain, in order that he can go ahead and finance his next year's operation. At the same time it provides him with an income from the storage space he has built in order to accommodate the grain which the corporation has purchased. That storage space can also be used for other products as soon as the grain is removed. When the grain has eventually been delivered to the corporation the farmer can then use the same storage space for feed grains, corn or anything else he may have on his farm.
Something of that nature certainly should be done in this country. That in itself would provide a measure of relief for the whole surplus situation, and would probably make the kind of legislation now under discussion unnecessary, because you would then have an orderly system under which the farmers would know that having produced their grain, they would be paid for it in cash, and if it was necessary to store it on the farm for any length of time they would be compensated for the storage they had to provide.
Those are some of the things we have been advocating for a long time, and on this occasion I appeal particularly to my good friends from the province of Manitoba who represent rural ridings. I ask them to support the idea of cash advances, because their attitude has always been a matter of sorrow to me.
Grain
When I go out on the prairies between sessions I sometimes drop in on public meetings where various members of the Liberal party are speaking to the farmers. I listen to them and I hear them talk in such fine terms about the need for cash advances, and I say to myself that it would do so much more good if I could just pick them up while they are speaking, bring them back to the House of Commons and dump them down in their places so they could continue their speeches here. Somehow we do not hear these fine speeches in the house. They seem to be limited to Portage-Neepawa, Provencher or other parts of Manitoba. When these members enter the house it seems that the atmosphere of this place takes away all their enthusiasm.
After all, there is a testing time coming in the near future. This issue will have to be faced by these members, and if it is not faced in the house it will have to be faced by them in their constituencies. I think it might be better for their own peace of mind if they were to rise in their places, whether they come from Manitoba or Saskatchewan, and say to the government on the floor of the house that they do not consider this legislation adequate. It has been pronounced inadequate by the farm organizations, and as good representatives of the farmers it is the duty of these members to get up and so advise the government.
By doing so they would be performing a useful service. If they fail to do so I would not be too surprised if the Minister of Trade and Commerce got the impression that if his own supporters from the prairie provinces are not at all interested in improving upon this legislation then it must be good enough, and the government will just go on merrily from year to year and keep extending it with all its inadequacies and do nothing about cash advances.
Therefore I invite these hon. members to take part in the debate and state in the house the same opinions I have heard them state at public meetings in their own constituencies. That is all I ask them to do. If they do that faithfully I am sure the Minister of Trade and Commerce will withdraw this inadequate resolution and probably early next week will bring in a resolution to provide for cash advances on farm-stored grain, with the government prepared to absorb the interest in the way the farm organizations have demanded.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am afraid I cannot be quite as optimistic as the last speaker in believing that the minister will withdraw this legislation, though I quite agree that is the very best thing the minister

Grain
could do in the interests of the farmers and then bring down something more along the line the farmers are requesting.
One of the peculiarities of this parliament has been that during a period of so-called prosperity the government has been quite busy passing bill after bill to help stampede the people of the country further and further into debt.
Last year we raised the ceiling on loans under the Small Loans Act, the Industrial Development Bank Act and the National Housing Act. Then there was special treatment for agriculture, because the government realized that agriculture was not in as prosperous a position as other industries. Instead of trying to bring about conditions that would make it possible for agriculture to enjoy the same level of prosperity as other groups, the government merely took steps to make it possible for the farmers to plunge further and further into debt.
So we have had a succession of bills, a bill to increase the amount of money that can be borrowed under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, a bill to increase the amount of money that may be borrowed from the farm loan board, and now this prairie grain producers interim financing bill. This session we have increased the capital of the farm loan board so the board can lend more money. Now we have this bill which makes it possible for the banks to lend $3,000 to a farmer instead of $1,500. In other words it guarantees the banks against loss, and I think there is far more concern being shown for the bankers under this legislation than there is for the farmers.
It is quite evident that in the past few years agriculture has not enjoyed the same level of prosperity as other industries, and the government has done very little to help the farmers in that regard apart from paying the carrying charges on wheat carried over in the year in excess of 178 million bushels. The government apparently thinks it has fulfilled its obligation when it helps the farmers to go into debt which, of course, increases farm costs by expanding the interest charges the farmers have to pay.
We all realize that the farmers are obliged to sell their wheat through the wheat board. Unfortunately, owing to the government failing to adjust their marketing policies to handle a succession of large crops, the marketing channels for wheat have become congested. It is rather interesting to note that five months after the end of the crop year, on January 4 of this year, we see a situation in Alberta where two points were on a unit, 179 points were on 1 bushel, 245 points were on 2 bushels and 155 points were on 3 bushels.
[Mr. Quelch.l
That, mind you, was the situation five months after the end of the crop year.
How were those farmers expected to carry on in a situation of that kind? Naturally they were obliged to borrow money, unless they were in the fortunate position of having been able to build up a reserve. Some of the older farmers may be in that happy position, but unfortunately many of the younger farmers and veterans are finding it extremely difficult to finance. The Alberta Wheat Pool Budget of January 25, referring to a situation in the south, under the heading "Grain Not Being Moved", had this to say:
According to reports coming from the southern part of Alberta, farmers are not satisfied with the movement of grain from that area this year. They claim that promises by the wheat board to give extra consideration to points that wound up last year with low quotas have not been implemented.
I do not know whether or not the wheat board actually made that promise, but certainly we had the assurance of the Minister of Trade and Commerce last year that points which had a low quota at the end of the last crop year would be given special consideration this year. I have not found that to be the case. I made an investigation of a number of points where they had a low quota at the end of the crop year last year, and I found that they were on a low quota this year.
That fact did not have anything to do with the type of grain they had for sale. Hence those farmers naturally feel that they are being discriminated against, and they are not at all satisfied with the suggestion that legislation of this kind will meet their situation. As I say, as a consequence of this situation we have a great many of the young farmers leaving the farms because they find they can get a higher standard of living and far shorter hours of labour by going into other industries.
The western grain conference in 1956 urged the government to make cash advances against grain up to 50 per cent of the estimated delivery quota. I think that was a very moderate suggestion and a very fair one. Ever since that time the farm organizations have been making similar suggestions. I think the Gordon commission made one fairly good suggestion in this regard, though I am not by any means endorsing the majority of their proposals. However, at least they recognized that if all farmers were not able to deliver the same amount of wheat, there should be an obligation on the part of the wheat board or the government to accept enough wheat from the farmers so the quotas can be evened up. I think that was quite a fair suggestion.
We believe a number of steps should be taken to remove the present congestion of wheat. First of all we believe that there

should be an expansion of storage. If there were an expansion of storage it would be possible for farmers to deliver more wheat and legislation of this kind would not be needed. In addition, cash advances against grain stored on the farm would not be as important.
Then we feel there should be an expansion of sales by a number of methods such as, for instance, the acceptance of foreign currency, barter and, in the case of dire distress, gifts. I know the Minister of Trade and Commerce has never been sympathetic to that idea. Nevertheless the United States are continuing to expand their sales of wheat and the thing the Minister of Trade and Commerce prophesied would happen has not happened. The Minister of Trade and Commerce prophesied that if the government were to sell more wheat by the acceptance of foreign currency or barter, they would sell less wheat for dollars. What do we find in the United States? We find that they are expanding their sales for foreign currency and that they are at the same time expanding their dollar sales. Hence the main objections which the minister raised to that proposal seem to be melting away.
If the government are not prepared to take steps that will make it possible for the farmers to deliver more wheat, I think they would be justified in introducing legislation which would make it possible to divert land from the production of wheat and utilize it in other fields along lines similar to what was done in -connection with the soil bank in the United States, or under legislation that we had in this country during the war. I think that legislation was called the Wheat Acreage Reduction Act. Under it farmers were paid to sow land down to grass and into pasture, etc.
If there is a feeling that our reserve of wheat is getting too large and that the situation is going to continue, surely the logical thing would be to encourage the farmers to put some of their land into grasses which would help build up the fertility of the soil, so that when the day arrived when more wheat was needed we would have the land in good shape, ready for the cultivator, and it could be put back into cultivation and the need supplied.
I think the immediate need is for the government to adopt a system of cash advances, that is if they are really interested in providing legislation that the farmers want. The government could also help to remove the discrimination that exists in the quotas by raising the price of wheat so much a month, a cent a bushel a month or more, on the amount of .wheat that is going to be
Grain
delivered under the quota. We had legislation of that kind in operation some years ago, and it at least helped to remove the discrimination that existed as between farmers who could deliver their wheat and those farmers who were not able to do so. A program of that kind, of course, would apply only to the wheat that was going to be delivered under the quota in that year.
The main objections I have to the present legislation are first, that it provides for no interest charge. The old act provided for an interest charge of 5 per cent. None of us knows what interest rate is to be incurred under this legislation. The minister says it is too far ahead to say what the interest charge should be. From that I do not suppose we have any right to believe the minister intends to reduce the interest rate. I think everything would indicate that if the interest rate is changed it will be to a higher interest rate.
I want to point out that already, today, the farmers of this country are being severely penalized as a result of the government's monetary policy. That monetary policy today is to boost interest rates, no doubt in order to encourage foreign investment in this country, which has the direct result of appreciating the dollar. The Canadian dollar is quoted at about $1.04 in United States funds. I believe it has been as high as $1.05.
What effect has that on agriculture? It means that farmers today are obliged to take 7 cents a bushel less for their wheat as a result of government monetary policy. The governor of the Bank of Canada points out that having an appreciated dollar helps to reduce the cost of living in this country, and that the people as a whole benefit as a result of the price of imports being lowered. But what is the effect upon agriculture? The effect is that the farmers are penalized by being obliged to take a lower price for their exports. If it is to the advantage of the general Canadian economy to have an appreciated dollar, then it seems to me the government is under some obligation to -compensate the farmers for the penalty imposed upon them as a result of appreciating the Canadian dollar. I would point out that the appreciation of the Canadian dollar has practically wiped out the advantage of the government paying the cost of grain in storage.
Another point in this bill upon which I should like to comment is that if a farmer has not been able to repay his whole loan he cannot get a new loan. It stands to reason that if a farmer cannot sell his wheat, he is not going to be able to repay his loan. Then why should he be debarred from taking the new loan if, as a result of government policy, he is not able to sell his wheat

Grain
in order to repay his first loan? I think some consideration should be given to allowing a farmer to take an additional loan in cases where he has not been allowed to deliver more than a very small amount of wheat.
It is quite evident that there is not any enthusiasm in the country for this legislation. I was frankly amazed when the minister stated that all farm organizations had asked for this legislation to be introduced. We have had a number of farm organizations in Ottawa during this session, and every delegation that has appeared before our group has been asked, "What is your attitude toward this legislation; do you think we should support it or not?" We have not had a single delegate tell us that this legislation was of any great value. Several, I think, suggested the best thing we could do would be to oppose it. Not one delegate suggested that we should support this legislation; so if these organizations told the minister they were in favour of the legislation then apparently they are telling two different stories, because they have not given that story to this group when they have appeared before us.
They still feel that the only solution to this problem is cash advances. We feel that the government is under an obligation to introduce legislation which will make cash advances available until such time as adequate storage has been provided and sales expanded, which will make it possible for the farmers to bring about an orderly marketing of their wheat.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO ACT EXTENDING APPLICATION, FIXING INTEREST AND INCREASING MAXIMUM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to join with the other members of the C.C.F. party as well as those in the other opposition political groups in the house in an attempt to convince the government of the desirability of replacing this legislation, which the minister is introducing, by other legislation to provide for a system of cash advances. I think the very fact that the government has been forced to introduce this unpopular legislation is an indication of the ineptitude of this government.
As indicated by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort, this is just a part of the larger problem which is confronting Canadian farmers. Indeed, I think this legislation is illustrative of the horse and buggy thinking of the government. In fact, when I think of this type of legislation, and the bankruptcy of the government, I think back to the thirties when we were farming with horses and the one obstacle we had in the field as we drove the horses down it was the ever-present danger of the horse stepping into a badger hole. Here we have the government preparing another badger hole in an

effort to wreck the efforts of the farmers in carrying out their operations.
I can notice some similarity between the government's policy in connection with farmers and the operation of the planning and works department of the city of Ottawa. I hope the government is not getting its ideas from the Ottawa road department, because there are pot holes in the city streets which would make a self-respecting western badger very envious. Each year the city works department goes around sprinkling a little bit of sand and gravel in the hole to make it look a little better, and each succeeding year it is chopped out again by the traffic. Here we have the government smoothing over this eruption in the western economy, the difficulty due to cash shortage, with a proposal for bank loans which no more meets the problem than does the patching of the roads in the city of Ottawa.
I think it is apparent that what is required is a rebuilding of our agricultural program. Perhaps I have given the government too much credit by implying that there was an agricultural program. Indeed, what is required is an agricultural program which will fit into all aspects of the Canadian economy, an agricultural program that will be geared to maximum production and maximum returns to the farmers of Canada. If we had such a system it would not be necessary to introduce this palliative of bank loans to remedy the severe cash shortage which is confronting western farmers.
I think an indication of this ineptitude is the fact that we have the largest grain carryover on record. The minister has stated that this has been due entirely to the bounties of nature. I cannot agree with that. I will say that in part it is due to the bounties of nature, due to the rainfall and the good climatic conditions we may have experienced, but it has been built up as a result of the failure of the government to apply an agricultural policy that would allow farmers to go into the production of other things rather than straight grain farming, where we have the security of the Canadian wheat board.
I think this legislation has been necessary because of the failure of this government to adopt realistic trade policies. Indeed, the delegates of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, at their annual convention this year, passed the following resolution, No. 5:
We recommend that the government of Canada should take all possible steps to develop trade arrangements involving increased imports of industrial goods from those countries which require substantial quantities of our agricultural products, and thus broaden the sales field available to the wheat board.

It is evident that the rank and file of the western farmers, the delegate body of the Saskatchewan wheat pool, are quite aware of the problems that are confronting us and are making suggestions which are continuously ignored by this government. The recent experience the farmers have undergone, of being forced to subsidize the Canadian millers so they could compete against the United States treasury in certain export markets, is another example of the shallow thinking of the government. The Minister of Trade and Commerce indicated that this action was necessary in order that Canadian wheat would find its way into the markets. In other words, because of the failure of this government to follow a realistic trade policy the wheat producers in western Canada are being forced to subsidize the millers by 4.5 cents to 8 cents a bushel.
I know what the minister's technique is in this connection. He will deny that the government has anything to do with it. In fact on page 1875 of Hansard for March 5, 1957, he said, in referring to the policy of subsidizing the Canadian millers, that this whole program was established by the wheat board. Previously, as recorded at page 1698 of Hansard for February 27, 1957, when the minister was asked a question about the allocation of box cars, he replied:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, priority has been given to those points. That was my instruction to the wheat board, and I know that the wheat board has been attempting to carry out that instruction.
There we have it. If the policy the wheat board is following happens to be favourable to this government they are only too anxious to take credit for it, but if it is an unpopular policy they again make the officials of the wheat board the whipping boy for government inefficiency.
The government has continued to compound the difficulties of the wheat board and of the farmers by refusing to appoint a transport controller.
It is part and parcel of this same problem of the need for cash advances owing to the inability of the farmers to market their grain. It was apparent that the former transport controller was under criticism from western farm organizations because of his failure to use the powers which he had to ensure that box cars were fairly allocated. His term of office expired at the close of shipping last year, and the government has just left the office vacant. It has now announced that this very difficult and onerous job is to be thrust upon the shoulders of the Canadian wheat board, so they will come under more difficulty in their operations.
Grain
In introducing this resolution the minister stated that he had never introduced a resolution that had met with such unanimous approval from farm organizations. I do not know where the minister gets his information, because I have resolutions passed by those same farm organizations which give me an indication of their thinking, and I should like to relay this information to hon. members.
We will go back to the annual report of the Saskatchewan wheat pool for 1953. One resolution dealing with their future policy states:
To bring into effect a plan of interim farm financing which will enable farmers unable to deliver grain at country elevators, to secure cash advances against grain in store on the farm.
In 1955 we have this same organization passing the following resolution:
That the organizations participating in this conference urge the government of Canada to make immediate provision for advances to farmers on grain in store on the farm; and further, that these advances should be up to one-half of the value of normal delivery expected and should be repayable on the basis of one-half of the value of each delivery made by the farmer.
This is another indication of the thinking of the delegate body of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. We find that at that same meeting instructions were given to the board of directors, as indicated in the resolution passed at that meeting, as follows:
That the board of directors give consideration to drafting a plan that will permanently meet the need for advances on farm-stored grain, and that this plan be presented to the next annual meeting of delegates.
We find that at that annual meeting the delegate body again favoured a system of cash advances on grain on the farm, as is outlined in resolution No. 8:
That cash advances should be made by elevator companies operating under a special line of credit, guaranteed by the federal Department of Finance.
They went on to outline a system of cash advances which they wanted this government to adopt. The interprovincial farm union council, in their memorandum on grain presented to the federal-provincial agricultural conference on December 3, had this to say:
The bank loan legislation implemented last year has not provided a solution. We feel a permanent system of cash advances must be instituted to provide financial assistance to farmers during periods when, due to congested facilities, they cannot deliver their produce.
There we have representative thinking of the farmers of western Canada, and I am quite certain that if you were again to ask the delegate body of the Saskatchewan wheat pool and the members of the interprovincial farm union council for their opinions they would reaffirm this declaration.
We find that the problem is of such far-reaching importance in western Canada that it has received the consideration of organized

Grain
labour. They have found that the cash shortage of farmers in western Canada is creating a hardship for them as well, and in the merger convention that the Saskatchewan federation of labour held in Regina in November of last year they, too, passed a resolution requesting cash advances on farm-stored grain through the elevator system. We can take it right down to the municipal authorities. At the annual meeting of the rural municipality of Newcombe No. 260, held on October 25, 1957, the following resolution was passed unanimously by the ratepayers present:
That we strongly protest the interest-bearing bank loan scheme as a solution to the farmers' financial plight and that we recommend a policy of interest-free advances on farm-stored grain.
It is apparent then, Mr. Chairman, that the farm organizations, the labour organizations and the farmers themselves are overwhelmingly in favour of a system of cash advances to deal with the present shortage in western Canada. This same indication was given by the select special committee on marketing and farm income of the Saskatchewan legislature. One of the recommendations for short-term policies recommended cash advances. It reads:
That a system of cash advances consisting of prepayment on farm-stored grain be implemented immediately, particularly in areas where grain delivery quotas have been unusually restrictive.
There we have the provincial representatives of the people of Saskatchewan in 1956 giving an indication that they too are overwhelmingly in favour of cash advances. The hon. member for Acadia referred to the preliminary report of the Gordon commission which indicated that a system of cash advances should be inaugurated. The report states in part.
Farmers' needs for cash income could be met by a system of intermediate payments based on the rate of delivery over the crop year.
By that I am not indicating my support for the report of the Gordon commission itself on wheat, but I did notice, Mr. Chairman, that this same indication was commented upon favourably by the president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. Now, if you add up all the evidence I have placed on the record, indicating a desire for cash advances and opposition to the system of bank loans, I fail to see how the minister can state that he has brought this in on the recommendations of farm organizations. I have quoted the resolutions from those farm organizations, and I claim that those resolutions reflect the thinking of the rank and file of the membership of those same organizations.
It was pointed out by members of this group that the C.C.F. stand is that of requesting a system of cash advances rather

than bank loans. It was indicated that the problem is larger than that which can be solved by temporary palliatives, and that you cannot cure the economic ills of the country by introducing a system of cash advances.
It was also indicated by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort that cash advances fit into the proposal for orderly marketing which we in this group have been advocating. We have been the strongest proponents of orderly marketing through the Canadian wheat board, and we feel that the system of cash advances would fit very well into this system. On the other hand, the bank loans do not fit into this proposal. I say the cash advances fit into this proposal because they would play an effective role in distributing the income of the farmers over the year, and would allow them to compensate for the unequal quota position which they are experiencing at the present time.
The hon. member who led off for this group indicated that one-third of the marketing points in western Canada were on a 2-bushel quota.
It is apparent that we have some marketing points on a 2-bushel quota and some on a 5-bushel quota, a situation that developed and was encouraged by the government last year. On former occasions when each marketing point had the same quota there was not this same urgency for this type of remedial action. It is most unfair for one farmer to receive a return on five bushels to the acre when another is receiving a return on only two bushels to the acre.
This can be corrected by a system of cash advances rather than a system of bank loans which does nothing more than increase consumer indebtedness. That is something to which all hon. members of this house should give consideration, because there has been a serious increase in consumer indebtedness, and bank loans only contribute to compounding it. In fact, in 1950 consumer indebtedness in Canada was $1,034,000,000, and it has now doubled to a colossal $2,395,000,000. This is an indication of the path we are following.
The record of these bank loans is not one which would receive our hearty commendation, because we find that since its inception the average loan as at the end of January, 1957, according to my computation was $704.16. The average loan in the first period was $764.45, when the maximum amount was $1,500. There is apparently something wrong with this program other than the maximum amount of the loans. We find that the average loan in the second period from November, 1956, to January, 1957, dropped $70 to stand at $694.87. The cost to the government and to the banks since the inception of the bank

loan scheme has been nothing. It is true that there is still an amount of $140,000 outstanding for the first period, but it will be recovered in following years.
The government apparently are not so satisfied with their legislation, as is indicated by their grave tardiness in renewing it by order in council this fall. If there was such a serious cash shortage as the minister states-and indeed there was a serious cash shortage-why did not the government take some action instead of sleeping at the switch until Thursday, November 29, when the order in council was passed renewing the legislation? They had the power under the act to renew it from October 1, but instead they sat idly by until November 29, 1956.
The fancy footwork on the part of the minister in attempting to popularize this measure by changing the date from October 1 to September 1 will have little appeal to western farmers. As was pointed out, at September 1 most farmers are only starting to harvest their crops, and according to the regulations which are printed in the Canada Gazette they are required to indicate the quantity of threshed grain at the time of their application. If a farmer lived in one of those areas that had been flooded out or sustained a crop failure in the previous year he would be unable to benefit by virtue of the fact that this starts on September 1; but more dangerous than that is the fact that this measure encourages the indebtedness of farmers.
I feel the fact that the government is extending this legislation is an admission of the continued failure of its policies. It is apparent that we are going to experience the same congestion next year that we experienced this year, and we will have the same cash shortage next year that we have this year. These problems cannot be resolved by increasing the indebtedness of the farmers.
Another feature I observed which indicates that the government is experiencing difficulty concerning the operation of the act was in relating it to the same type of legislation passed in previous years. In 1951 when the grain was out under the snow the government introduced legislation providing a 5J per cent interest rate and a $1,000 maximum loan, and the maximum amount of capital held by the government was $20 million. In 1956 the interest rate was lowered to 5 per cent and the maximum loan was increased by $500 to $1,500. Then the government felt it was necessary to increase the capital amount to $50 million. In 1957 in the legislation which the minister is proposing he has supposedly
Grain
doubled the amount. We do not know what the interest rate is to be, but he is quite convinced there is not going to be an increased demand for the loans because the capitalization is not to be changed.
We are opposing this legislation, as we did last year, because we honestly believe it prevents the adoption of sound legislation to provide cash advances. I realize that the minister is quite capable of putting up straw men, donning a Sherlock Holmes hat and going around trying to find all kinds of evidence as to why the system of cash advances would not work. He is capitalizing on the difficulty he has in getting all the farm organizations in western Canada to agree to the letter of the proposal they want for cash advances.
According to information that was given to me by the delegate body and many of the directors of farm organizations, it is apparent that a system of cash advances is workable. I feel that as a federal government we owe something to the farmers of western Canada, and that we should bear the interest cost in order that their burden of debt should not be further compounded.
When farm organizations endeavour to improve upon this legislation they are put in the position of a quack doctor who is trying to decide whether he should administer a dose of castor oil or a dose of epsom salts to someone suffering from appendicitis. Both would be fatal. Similarly you cannot improve this legislation by changing the date from October to September and by increasing the maximum amount from $1,500 to $3,000. It is the basic legislation that is at fault, particularly in the way it fits into our economy.
I would like to reiterate the closing remarks of the hon. member for Dauphin, who appealed to the government to give this matter further consideration, to withdraw this legislation and introduce a system of cash advances which will prove universally popular in western Canada.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.

subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY, NOVA SCOTIA
TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY, NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
1.	Which government is responsible for designating the route of the trans-Canada highway in Nova Scotia?
2.	What route was specified in the original agreement between the federal and provincial governments?
3.	Was any change made in the route since the original agreement was signed?
4.	If so, when, in what respect, and at whose request?
5.	Has the government of Nova Scotia requested further changes in the location of the route?
6.	If so, when, and in what respect?
Answer by:	Mr. Bourgei, Parliamentary
Assistant, for the Minister of Public Works:
1.	The government of the province of Nova Scotia, subject to approval by the federal government.
2.	Schedule "A" of the original agreement specified the route as follows:
"Generally from the New Brunswick-Nova Scotia border via route 4 to the strait of Canso, crossing the strait via the proposed causeway, and thence to the Newfoundland ferry terminal at North Sydney via a route to be determined as a result of further surveys.
The trans-Canada highway in Nova Scotia shall also include that portion of highway from the junction of the West river-Pictou road at route 4, to Pictou, and thence to the Prince Edward Island ferry terminal at Caribou."
3.	Yes.
4.	The government of the province of Nova Scotia requested a change of route which was incorporated in schedule "A" of the trans-Canada highway agreement, of September 4, 1956, as follows:
"From the New Brunswick-Nova Scotia border to Oxford, thence via route 4 to Sutherland river, thence via Merigomish, Arisag and Antigonish to the strait of Canso, crossing the strait via the causeway to Port Hastings; and thence via Whycocomagh and Baddeck to the Newfoundland ferry terminal at North Sydney. On the portion between Sutherland river and Antigonish, Canada's participation will be limited to a distance of 30.4 miles.
The trans-Canada highway in Nova Scotia shall also include that portion of highway from the junction of the West river-Pictou road at route 4, to Pictou, and thence to the Prince Edward Island ferry terminal at Caribou."
5.	Yes.
6.	A revision of schedule "A" of the agreement of September 4, 1956, was requested on February 5, 1957. The route specified is now as follows:
"The trans-Canada highway in Nova Scotia shall proceed generally from the New Brunswick-Nova Scotia border to Oxford; thence via route 4 to the strait of Canso, crossing the strait via the causeway to Port Hastings; thence via Whycocomagh, Baddeck and Little Bras d'Or to the Newfoundland ferry terminal at North Sydney.
The trans-Canada highway in Nova Scotia shall also include that portion of highway from the junction of the West river-Pictou road at route 4 to Pictou, and thence to the Prince Edward Island ferry terminal at Caribou."
